content: Upper back pain, also referred to as middle back pain or thoracic pain, is discomfort experienced in the region between the base of the neck and the top of the lumbar spine. The upper spine is structurally robust and stable, designed to support the weight of the upper body and to anchor the rib cage. The rib cage, in turn, provides a protective cavity for vital organs such as the heart and lungs, ensuring their proper function. The term thoracic pertains to the chest, and the thoracic spine constitutes the upper portion of the spinal column that corresponds to the chest area. This section of the spine consists of twelve vertebrae. The upper nine vertebrae in this region are each connected to a rib on either side. These ribs curve around the sides of the body and attach to the breastbone (sternum) at the front, forming a sturdy structure known as the thoracic cage. This cage serves to support and protect internal organs, including the heart, lungs, and liver. Upper back pain can arise from muscular issues, such as strain or injury to the muscles and ligaments in the area. These problems may result from insufficient muscle strength, poor posture, repetitive motion injuries, or trauma, such as a car accident or sports injury. Treatment for muscular strain in the upper back typically involves one or a combination of the following approaches: Exercise and physical therapy (both active and passive) Chiropractic or osteopathic manipulation Deep tissue massage or massage therapy Acupuncture Ice and/or heat therapy Pain medications, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) If a specific tender spot is identified, trigger point massage or injections may provide relief. Another potential cause of upper back pain is dysfunction in the joints that connect the vertebrae to the ribs. Treatment for joint-related issues often includes: Manual manipulation performed by an osteopathic physician or chiropractor Exercise and physical therapy Anti-inflammatory medications to manage pain A vertebral compression fracture can also lead to acute or chronic upper back pain. This is particularly relevant for women over the age of 50, as osteoporosis-related vertebral compression fractures should always be considered a possible cause of upper back pain in this demographic. Painful vertebral compression fractures may be managed with pain medications and rest, or through surgical interventions such as vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty. Less common causes of upper back pain include spinal disc herniation, degenerative disc disease, or trauma, such as a fall, that may result in a fractured vertebra within the thoracic spine.
